question.problem: Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y)={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨3,7⟩,$ respectively.
question.worked_solution:
The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that the function $f(x,y)={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨3,7⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3,7)-f(0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨3,7⟩-⟨0,1⟩) \\ ({7}^{2}-{3}^{2})-({1}^{2}-{0}^{2}) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,6⟩ \\ 39 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨-2x,2y⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨-2{c}_{1},2{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}39 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨3,6⟩ \\ 39 & =⟨-2{c}_{1},2{c}_{2}⟩\cdot ⟨3,6⟩ \\ 39 & =-6{c}_{1}+12{c}_{2} \\ 13 & =-2{c}_{1}+4{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-1}{7-1} & =\frac{x-0}{3-0} \\ \frac{y-1}{6} & =\frac{x}{3} \\ y-1 & =2x \\ y & =2x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =2{c}_{1}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the equation $-2{c}_{1}+4{c}_{2}=13,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{c}_{1}+4(2{c}_{1}+1) & =13 \\ -2{c}_{1}+8{c}_{1}+4 & =13 \\ 6{c}_{1} & =9 \\ {c}_{1} & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find ${c}_{2}=2{c}_{1}+1=4.$ So, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is $(\frac{3}{2},4).$
